claim: Central indirect taxes replaced by GST (CBIC): Central Excise Duty; Duties of Excise (Medicinal and Toilet Preparations); Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance); Additional Duties of Excise (Textiles and Textile Products); Additional Duties of Customs (commonly CVD); Special Additional Duty of Customs (SAD); Service Tax; cesses and surcharges relating to supply of goods or services.

State taxes subsumed (CBIC): State VAT; Central Sales Tax; Purchase Tax; Luxury Tax; Entry Tax (all forms); Entertainment Tax (except those levied by local bodies); taxes on advertisements; taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling; State cesses and surcharges relating to supply of goods or services.

GST applies to all goods and services except alcohol for human consumption; GST on crude, petrol, diesel, ATF and natural gas applies from a date to be recommended by the Council. GST was introduced on 1 July 2017.

source: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2272, 9 Dec 2024, Ministry of Finance (Dept of Revenue), Annexures A-C

claim: Compensation Act: s.2(1) defines the transition period as five years from a State's transition date; s.3 sets projected growth at 14% a year; s.4 takes the year ending 31 March 2016 as base year; s.6 projects revenue by applying that rate to base-year revenue; s.7(3) makes compensation the shortfall of actual revenue below projected revenue.
source: GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 (Act 15 of 2017, assent 12 Apr 2017), text on CBIC GST site
note: [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Cites fixed (14% and base year are ss.3-4). Old text said shortfall of actual over projected, which reversed the direction; s.7(3)(c) is projected minus actual.

claim: The revenue effect is also tied to the cess: the Compensation Act s.8 levies cess on specified goods, up to rates in the Schedule, and the cess is credited to a non-lapsable Compensation Fund in the public account of India (s.10).
